readings.title: Mrs. Redwing’s Speckled Egg
readings.challenge: Keep track of two things the Breezes do all morning: teasing and helping.
readings.focus: Playful mischief becomes a rescue when the Breezes use their tricks for someone in trouble.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Mrs. Redwing is a red-winged blackbird. Bulrushes are tall plants that grow in wet ground. On a farm a breakfast horn was blown to call people in to eat.
readings.contentNote: Farmer Brown hunts Johnny Chuck with a gun, and a boy sets out to take a bird’s eggs. Neither of them succeeds.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Mrs. Redwing’s Speckled Egg,” the whole chapter; opens “Old Mother West Wind came down from the Purple Hills in the golden light of the early…”; closes “…knew, that some day out of that pretty new speckled egg would come a wee baby Redwing.”.

questions.prompt: What do the Breezes do to Johnny Chuck at breakfast? Does he really mind?
facilitatorNotes: They snatch his corn leaf, pull his whiskers and rumple his hair. He pretends to be cross, but he loves them, and they warn him when Farmer Brown comes.
evidence: Johnny Chuck pretended to be very cross indeed, but really he didn’t mind a bit

questions.prompt: How do the Breezes keep Tommy Brown away from the nest? Retell the chase.
facilitatorNotes: They take turns blowing his straw hat away just as he reaches it, all the way across the meadow and the brook, and hang it in a thorn tree. By then he has forgotten the nest, and the breakfast horn calls him home.
evidence: Then they took turns
they hung the old straw hat in the middle of a thorn tree

questions.prompt: Why does Tommy Brown want the eggs? What do you think of his reason?
facilitatorNotes: “Just because they were pretty,” not because he needs them. Ask whether liking something is a reason to take it. Some children may say he does not understand that eggs hold baby birds.
evidence: just because they were pretty

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Redwing sing for joy at the end? What do she and the Breezes both know?
facilitatorNotes: That a baby Redwing will hatch from the speckled egg. They saved more than a pretty egg; they saved a bird to come.
evidence: some day out of that pretty new speckled egg would come a wee baby Redwing

readings.title: Why Grandfather Frog Has No Tail
readings.challenge: Hear a story told inside another story, and notice who is listening to it.
readings.focus: A made-up “why” story wraps around something true: tadpoles lose their tails as they grow into frogs.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Pollywogs, also called tadpoles, are baby frogs that live in water and have tails. Grandfather Frog’s tale of the proud King Frog is invented, but the change from tadpole to frog is real. To be vain is to be too proud of how you look.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Why Grandfather Frog Has No Tail,” the whole chapter; opens “Old Mother West Wind had gone to her day’s work, leaving all the Merry Little Breezes to…”; closes “…first and tell him that Farmer Brown was coming down on the Green Meadows with a gun.”.

questions.prompt: How can the Pollywogs be Grandfather Frog’s grandchildren when they look nothing like him?
facilitatorNotes: They are tadpoles, and tadpoles grow into frogs. The story says you would never guess unless someone told you.
evidence: They didn’t look the least bit like Grandfather Frog.

questions.prompt: When Grandfather Frog mentions hungry Mink, Billy Mink squirms and looks away. Why?
facilitatorNotes: Minks eat young frogs, and Billy feels caught. Grandfather Frog makes his point right in front of him.
evidence: squirmed uneasily and looked away guiltily

questions.prompt: What did the King Frog do all day, and why did Mother Nature take his tail?
facilitatorNotes: He ate, slept and admired his tail, and soon all the Frogs copied him. She took the thing he was vain about.
evidence: He did nothing at all but eat and sleep and admire his tail.

questions.prompt: Grandfather Frog says that people who do nothing worth while are “of no use.” Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: The story is hard on the Frogs. Some children will say everyone matters, even when resting or playing; others will say the Frogs’ real fault was thinking only of themselves. Both views can point to the words.
evidence: people who do nothing worth while in this world are of no use and there is little room for them

readings.title: How Reddy Fox Was Surprised
readings.challenge: Follow Johnny Chuck’s feelings as they change: lost, frightened, furious, then pleased.
readings.focus: A small animal’s sudden anger turns a bully’s trick around.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Johnny Chuck is a woodchuck, a plump animal that lives in a burrow. Bowser is a farm hound, a hunting dog. A “’fraid-cat” is a teasing name for someone who is scared.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “How Reddy Fox Was Surprised,” the whole chapter; opens “Johnny Chuck and Reddy Fox lived very near together on the edge of the Green Meadows.…”; closes “And this is the way that Reddy Fox was surprised and that Johnny Chuck found his way home.”.

questions.prompt: What had Johnny Chuck’s mother told him, and what did he do?
facilitatorNotes: Never to go out of sight of the door. He forgot and kept walking after patches that only looked like clover.
evidence: his mother had told him never to go out of sight of the door

questions.prompt: Johnny thinks he can’t be lost while Mr. Sun winks at him. Why doesn’t that work?
facilitatorNotes: The sun keeps moving across the sky and cannot show the way home; and Johnny falls asleep anyway. Accept either reason.
evidence: So long as I can see great round, red Mr. Sun and he winks at me I can’t be lost

questions.prompt: Reddy Fox expected Johnny to run. What does Johnny do instead, and how does he look?
facilitatorNotes: He chases Reddy, chattering, with every hair standing up so that he looks twice his size.
evidence: so that he seemed twice as big as he really was

questions.prompt: The last line says this is how Johnny Chuck found his way home. How did chasing Reddy get him there?
facilitatorNotes: Reddy ran straight home and passed Johnny’s house on the way, so Johnny followed him back without knowing it.
evidence: going home he passed the house of Johnny Chuck

readings.title: Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes — the broken eggs
readings.challenge: Collect clues the way a detective would, before anyone says who did it.
readings.focus: A mystery begins: someone has broken Mrs. Grouse’s eggs in the night, and Peter Rabbit looks closely.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. This is an invented “why” story; real skunks are simply born striped. Mrs. Ruffed Grouse is a woodland bird that nests on the ground. Buff is a pale yellow-brown. Old Dame Nature rules over the meadow folk in these stories.
readings.contentNote: A mother bird’s eggs are broken and eaten in the night. She is frightened but escapes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes,” from the start to the meadow folk gathering at the Great Pine; opens “Jimmy Skunk, as everybody knows, wears a striped suit, a suit of black and white. There…”; closes “…Mrs. Ruffed Grouse sat beside her empty nest, with all the broken shells about her.”.

questions.prompt: Long ago in this story, why could no one prove who did mischief at night?
facilitatorNotes: Jimmy Skunk’s coat was all black, so he could not be seen in the dark. Keep this clue for tomorrow.
evidence: his coat was so black that in the darkness of the night it was not visible at all

questions.prompt: What does Peter Rabbit do after he hears Mrs. Grouse’s story?
facilitatorNotes: He searches the ground carefully, behind the tree and under the bushes, and then whispers what he found to Johnny Chuck.
evidence: Peter Rabbit looked the ground over very carefully.

questions.prompt: How does Jimmy Skunk act when Peter and Johnny come to his house? Does anything seem odd?
facilitatorNotes: He is in bed in the morning, sleepy and cross, says “Too bad!” with a yawn, and has “other business.” Some children will already suspect him; others will not yet. Both are fair at this point.
evidence: said Jimmy Skunk, and yawned sleepily
he had some other business that morning

questions.prompt: Who do you think broke the eggs? Which clue makes you think so?
facilitatorNotes: A prediction: accept any guess that names a clue from the story, and come back to it tomorrow.
evidence: Jimmy Skunk was in bed. He was very sleepy and very cross

readings.title: Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes — the meeting at the Great Pine
readings.challenge: Put the clues together, the way Old Dame Nature does, to reach an answer.
readings.focus: Questions and evidence, not guessing, uncover the egg thief, and his punishment fits the way he hid.
readings.context: Recap: someone broke and ate Mrs. Grouse’s eggs in the night. Peter Rabbit searched the ground, and Jimmy Skunk was strangely sleepy that morning. Now Old Dame Nature has called all the meadow folk to the Great Pine. A culprit is the one who did a wrong thing; to accuse is to say someone did it; descendants are children, grandchildren and so on.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes,” from the arrival of the meadow folk to the end of the chapter; opens “Reddy Fox, Peter Rabbit, Johnny Chuck, Billy Mink, Little Joe Otter, Jerry Muskrat, Hooty…”; closes “And this is why that to this day Jimmy Skunk wears a striped suit of black and white.”.

questions.prompt: What does Jimmy Skunk say and do when he arrives at the meeting? Why might he act this way?
facilitatorNotes: He looks sorry, tells Mrs. Grouse how bad he feels, and loudly demands that the culprit be punished. A guilty animal might act extra innocent.
evidence: he loudly demanded that the culprit should be found out and severely punished

questions.prompt: Name the clues. What does each one point to?
facilitatorNotes: Three long black hairs point to a black coat; yellow whiskers to egg yolk; sleepiness to being out all night; and Mother West Wind saw a black shadow going toward Jimmy’s house.
evidence: three long black hairs
It MIGHT be the yolk of an egg
People who have been out all night

questions.prompt: Why does Old Dame Nature ask everyone questions instead of just saying who did it?
facilitatorNotes: So everyone hears the evidence and works it out together. Some children may say she wanted to give Jimmy a chance to speak; she does ask him for his answer.
evidence: What have you to say for yourself?

questions.prompt: Why are stripes the right punishment for Jimmy Skunk, in this story?
facilitatorNotes: His black coat hid him at night; a striped coat is always seen and marks him as untrusted. Some children will find it unfair that his descendants must wear stripes too. That is worth talking about.
evidence: that when you move about in the night you will always be visible
henceforth you and your descendants shall wear a striped coat

readings.title: Reddy Fox Goes Fishing
readings.challenge: Compare what Reddy Fox says he can do with what actually happens.
readings.focus: Showing off brings a fall, and Johnny Chuck, who stays home, gets the last word.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Trout are fish that live in cool streams. A mink is a slim brown animal that swims and catches fish. A kingfisher is a bird that dives for fish.
readings.contentNote: Billy Mink catches a little trout to take home, and Reddy Fox falls into the pool and swallows water before he crawls out. At the end Mother Fox waits with a switch, a thin stick once used to punish children.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Reddy Fox Goes Fishing,” the whole chapter; opens “One morning when Mr. Sun was very, very bright and it was very, very warm, down on the…”; closes “And this is all I am going to tell you about how Reddy Fox went fishing.”.

questions.prompt: Reddy Fox tries to get Johnny Chuck to come. What does Johnny keep saying, and why?
facilitatorNotes: “Can’t,” because his mother told him not to play with Reddy Fox. He even turns away so he cannot watch Reddy’s tricks.
evidence: said good little Johnny Chuck again, and turned away

questions.prompt: Why can Billy Mink catch a fish when Reddy Fox cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Billy keeps out of sight of Mr. and Mrs. Trout and then dives in fast; Reddy reached in where everyone could see him. Billy can also swim.
evidence: Billy Mink took care, such very great care, that Mr. Trout and Mrs. Trout should not see him

questions.prompt: What does Reddy dream about, and how does the dream end?
facilitatorNotes: That he has a waterproof coat like Billy’s and can swim and fish, and then he really does roll into the pool.
evidence: He dreamed that he had a nice little brown coat that was waterproof

questions.prompt: When Reddy comes home, Johnny Chuck asks why he doesn’t turn somersaults now. Is Johnny being fair?
facilitatorNotes: He is teasing back with Reddy’s own showing-off. Some children will say Reddy earned it; others that Johnny is gloating. Mother Fox’s switch shows Reddy has more trouble waiting.
evidence: Why don’t you turn somersaults, and jump over your shadow

readings.title: Jimmy Skunk Looks for Beetles
readings.challenge: Listen for the pattern that repeats, and notice when it changes.
readings.focus: Polite words do not make up for careless paws, and a trick turns back on the trickster.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Beetles are insects with hard wing-covers; real skunks do dig and hunt for them. Mr. Toad and Striped Chipmunk are neighbours whose homes are under bark and inside an old stump.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Jimmy Skunk Looks for Beetles,” the whole chapter; opens “Jimmy Skunk opened his eyes very early one morning and peeped out of his snug little…”; closes “…teach him a lesson, for Jimmy Skunk had found some beetles and was eating his breakfast.”.

questions.prompt: What does Jimmy Skunk ask everyone he meets? Say it with him.
facilitatorNotes: “Have you seen any beetles?” And after each accident: “I won’t do it again.” Let the child join the repeated lines.
evidence: Have you seen any beetles?

questions.prompt: Jimmy is always polite. Is he also careful? What happens to his neighbours’ homes?
facilitatorNotes: He pulls the roof off Mr. Toad’s house and the side off Striped Chipmunk’s, then steps right over them. His words are polite but his paws are careless; some children will say he means no harm.
evidence: pulling the roof off my house
pulling the side off my house

questions.prompt: What is the “little black string” really? Did Peter Rabbit know?
facilitatorNotes: Mr. Black Snake’s tail. Peter says he thinks there are beetles there, but his laughing suggests he guessed. Either reading fits.
evidence: The string Jimmy Skunk had pulled was Mr. Black Snake’s tail

questions.prompt: How does the ending turn the joke around? Who ends up in trouble, and who gets breakfast?
facilitatorNotes: Peter laughs and is chased by the snake; slow, polite Jimmy calmly finds his beetles.
evidence: for Jimmy Skunk had found some beetles and was eating his breakfast
